title: Browser Information Discovery
summary: Browser information discovery is a reconnaissance step in which an adversary reads the data browsers keep for each user profile, including bookmarks, history, saved credentials, autofill entries, cookies, download records and extension lists. This material is valuable beyond privacy: history and bookmarks expose the internal hosts, administrative dashboards, ticketing tools and code repositories an organisation uses, which sharpens later targeting, while saved credentials can be reused directly or combined with credentials-in-files hunting to widen access. The data lives in per-user profile directories as SQLite databases and JSON files, with locations that vary by platform and browser, so collection usually means copying or querying whole profile folders rather than any single well-known file. Because the files belong to the signed-in user, ordinary file and database read telemetry is the primary evidence: a process other than the browser reading those profile paths, bulk file copies from a profile directory, or archive creation over a browser data folder. The discriminator against legitimate activity is the reader: browsers, backup agents and profile sync services touch these files constantly, whereas command shells, scripting hosts, remote management tooling and unsigned binaries appearing as the reader are anomalous and worth investigating alongside any subsequent authentication attempts.

beginner.definition: Browsers keep a record of what each person does. They store bookmarks, page history, saved passwords and filled-in forms. Browser information discovery means an attacker reads those files to learn about you and your workplace.
beginner.whyItMatters: These files are not secret, so they are easy to forget. History and bookmarks show which internal sites and tools your team uses. Saved logins can open other systems directly. If you ignore this step, an attacker learns where to strike next without guessing.
howItWorks: Browsers save what you do in files stored inside your own user profile folder on the computer.
Those files hold bookmarks, page history, saved passwords, cookies and the entries used to fill in forms.
The data sits in small databases. On Windows they usually live under the AppData folder inside your profile.
An attacker who already has your account can simply copy those files, because they belong to your user.
Reading the history and bookmarks shows which internal sites, tools and dashboards your team depends on.
Saved logins then point the attacker at more systems, so this step often comes before deeper attacks.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat with a noticeboard beside the front door. Pinned to it are takeaway menus, a note with the wifi password, and a list of who holds a key to the roof. A guest who reads that board learns a great deal without opening a single locked door. The board is not secret, so nobody thinks to hide it. Your browser files are that board, because they describe where you go and how you get in.
takeaways: Browser profile files can be read by anything running as your user account.
History and bookmarks point at internal systems, so they guide an attacker.
Saved logins inside a browser are a direct path to more accounts.

objectives: Describe the kinds of data that browsers store for each user profile.
Explain why browsing history can reveal internal infrastructure to an attacker.
Explain how this technique differs from credential dumping, even when both touch saved passwords.
Identify which process and file access events reveal a browser profile being read by something other than the browser.
List the controls that reduce the value of data kept in browser profiles.
